analysis.one_liner: Lets small businesses opt out of almost any federal regulation issued after early 2009.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or a vote: it was introduced with zero cosponsors and referred to the House Small Business Committee, where it died when the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would let any small business simply notify a federal agency that it is exempt from any federal rule issued after January 20, 2009 — a cutoff that captures essentially every Obama-era regulation. In exchange, the business would have to label its products as no longer covered by the rule and mention the exemption in its communications, with penalties if it failed to do that. Only Defense and Homeland Security rules certified as necessary for U.S. security could not be avoided. The bill was referred to the House Small Business Committee and never moved again.
analysis.who_benefits: Small businesses that want to shed the cost of complying with federal rules on consumer protection, product safety, financial practices, workplace standards, or the environment. Any firm that meets the Small Business Act definition of a 'small business concern' could opt out of every qualifying rule at once.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Small businesses seeking to skip regulations

how_it_helps.text: Any small business could send one written notice to a federal agency and become exempt from that agency's rules 30 days later, effective across consumer, financial, labor, environmental, and product rules issued after January 20, 2009.
The only carve-out is for Defense or Homeland Security rules that those secretaries certify are necessary for U.S. security; every other rule is fair game.

The business's only ongoing obligation is to label affected products and mention the exemption in communications, so customers are told a product is 'no longer subject' to a rule but not what protection they have lost.

analysis.who_pays: Consumers and workers who deal with opting-out businesses. A family buying food, a loan, a product, or a service from a small firm that has opted out would lose whatever protection the rule provided — safety testing, honest labeling, limits on lending or collection practices, or workplace standards — with nothing in its place.

drawbacks.text: The exemption would strip protections from anything a rule covered — product safety, truthful labeling, consumer lending limits, environmental limits, and workplace standards — for any firm small enough to qualify, with customers left to figure out from a label what protections are gone.

The bill's own penalty clause undercuts its consumer-notice premise: a business that fails to comply with the labeling and notification requirements faces penalties as if it had never opted out, which means the only real check on abuse is a product sticker few shoppers would understand.

It would create an uneven playing field: a small firm could sell a product without meeting a rule that its larger competitor must still follow, giving the exempt firm a cost advantage rather than lowering risk for anyone.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For a small business owner, the compliance savings could be real. But the cost lands on the other side of the transaction: every protection a post-2009 rule provided — from safety and labeling to lending and workplace standards — would simply vanish for that firm's customers and workers, with only a vague 'no longer subject' notice in return. Because the opt-out applies to any and every rule at once, there is no weighing of which rules are burdensome versus which do their job. The bill offered a broad escape hatch rather than a targeted fix for regulatory overreach.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the House Small Business Committee on the same day in October 2011, and the committee never took it up — no hearing, no vote, nothing — so it expired when that Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Scott Garrett introduced the bill on October 6, 2011, and it was referred the same day to the House Committee on Small Business.
No cosponsors signed on, and the committee took no further action; the bill's entire history is the introduction and the referral.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill died without action, consumers kept the protections it would have let small businesses opt out of, and no regulation changed. The bill's sponsors and supporters gained nothing, and neither did the industries that would have used the exemption.

against.name: House Committee on Small Business
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on October 6, 2011 and took no further action — no hearing, no markup, no vote — before the Congress expired.

sides.party_line_note: There were no cosponsors and no votes, so no partisan pattern ever took shape; the bill was a solo Republican effort that drew no visible support from either party.

industries.note: The bill would hand any qualifying small business a one-notice exemption from every federal rule issued after January 20, 2009 — compliance costs saved, with the protection those rules gave customers and workers simply disappearing. The business's gain comes directly at the expense of the people it sells to or employs.

industries.industry: Consumer financial firms (small lenders, debt collectors and similar firms that meet SBA size standards)
industries.note: Consumer-protection rules issued after the 2008 financial crisis, including early post-crisis rulemakings, would be among the rules a small financial firm could elect out of, removing limits on lending and collection practices for its customers.

industries.industry: Large corporations subject to the same rules
industries.note: Big firms could not opt out, so a small competitor selling a product without meeting a mandatory rule would enjoy a cost advantage over them — an odd result for a bill framed as helping small business against big government.
